# Import Data - Basics {#import-data-in-r-basics}

## Introduction

In this chapter, we will learn to:

- read data from flat or delimited files
- handle column names/header
- skip text/info present before data
- specify column/variable types
- read specific columns/variables

We will use the following R packages:

```{r library1, message=FALSE}
library(readr)
```

## Delimiters

Before we start reading data from files, let us look at the different types of
delimiters we have to deal with. In general, it is good practice to look at the
file first, as you will then know which delimiter it uses.

### Comma Separated Values

```{r img1, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/mtcars_comma.png')
```

### Semi Colon Separated Values

```{r img2, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/mtcars_semicolon.png')
```

### Space Separated Values

```{r img3, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/mtcars_space.png')
```

### Tab Separated Values


## Read Data

Let us begin by reading data from a `csv` file using `read_csv()`. 

```{r csv}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb2.csv')
```

Great! If you see the above output, you have successfully read data into R. If 
you see an error message (which most of us see the first time we read data),
follow the instructions below:

- check the separator in the file and ensure it is a `comma`
- check the file name
- check the file path i.e. location of the file
- ensure that the file name or path is enclosed in single or double quotes

When you read data using `readr`, it displays the data type it has detected for 
each column in the data set. If you want to check the data types before reading
the data, use `spec_csv()`. We will learn to specify the column types in the next
section.

```{r spec_csv, message=FALSE}
spec_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb2.csv')
```

## Column Names

In some cases, files do not include column names or headers. If we do not say
so, `readr` treats the first row of the data as the column names. As we said
before, it is good practice to look at the data first to check for column names.

```{r img5, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/mtcars_comma.png')
```

```{r img6, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/mtcars_column_false.png')
```

We will first read the data set without indicating the presence or absence of
column names.

```{r col_names_1, message=FALSE}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb3.csv')
```

As you can see, in the absence of column names, `readr` has converted the 
first row of the data into the column names; the first data row is now the
header, so the names are numbers and one row is lost. 
If the column names are absent (i.e. the column names are provided in a 
separate file), use the `col_names` argument and set it to `FALSE`. `readr`
then leaves the first row as data and generates new column names.

```{r col_names, message=FALSE}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb3.csv', col_names = FALSE)
```

We may not always want the column names generated by `readr`; we can supply our
own instead. In such cases, use `col_names` to pass a vector of names, as in the
example below. Let us reread `hsb3` and specify column names.

```{r col_names2, message=FALSE}
cnames <- c("id", "gender", "race", "socio_economic_status", "school_type", "program", "read", "write", "math", "science", "socst")
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb3.csv', col_names = cnames)
```

## Skip Lines

In certain files, you will find information related to the data such as:

- the data source
- column names
- column description
- copyright etc.

The data appears below this text. While reading data from
such files, we need to skip all the rows where the text is present. If we do 
not skip them, `readr` will treat them as data.

```{r img7, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE, out.width="80%"}
knitr::include_graphics('img/mtcars_skip.png')
```

Let us read the data without skipping any rows and look at the result.

```{r skip_1, message=FALSE}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb4.csv')
```

Use the `skip` argument to indicate the number of rows to skip while 
reading data from a file. For example, if the file has contents other than data 
in the first few lines, we need to skip them before reading the data. In the 
example below, we skip the first 3 lines, which contain information about 
the data set that we do not need.

```{r skip, message=FALSE}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb4.csv', skip = 3)
```

## Maximum Lines 

Suppose the data file contains several thousand rows and we do not 
want to read all of them. What can we do in such cases? `readr` allows us to 
specify the maximum number of rows to read using the `n_max` argument.
If we want to read only 100 rows from a file, we set `n_max` 
equal to 100. In the next example, we will read the first 120 rows from the 
`hsb2` file. The last line of the output, `# ℹ 110 more
rows`, shows that only 120 rows were read from the 
file.

```{r n_max, message=FALSE}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb2.csv', n_max = 120)
```

## Column Types

In the output above, `readr` displays the column names and column types, 
followed by the first 10 rows of data. 
`readr` determines the type of each column from the first 1000 rows 
of data. The data can be of the following types:

- integer
- double (decimal point)
- logical (TRUE/FALSE)
- character (text/string)
- factor (categorical/qualitative)
- date/time

```{r img8, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/column_types_list_canva.png')
```

Before you read data from a file, use `spec_csv()` to see the data types as 
determined by `readr`. If it determines them correctly, go ahead and read the
data. Otherwise, we have to specify the types for all the columns we want to
read, not just for those whose type was wrongly determined by `readr`.

To specify the data types, we will use the `col_types` argument and supply it
a list of data types. The data types can be specified using:

- `col_integer()`
- `col_double()`
- `col_factor()`
- `col_logical()`
- `col_character()`
- `col_date()`
- `col_time()`
- `col_datetime()`

While specifying the data types we also need to specify the categories of the 
categorical/qualitative variable. To do that, we use the `levels` argument 
within `col_factor()`. Let us read data from the `hsb2.csv` file to understand
data type specification.

```{r col_types}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb2.csv', col_types = list(
  col_integer(), col_factor(levels = c("0", "1")), 
  col_factor(levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4")), col_factor(levels = c("1", "2", "3")), 
  col_factor(levels = c("1", "2")), col_factor(levels = c("1", "2", "3")),
  col_integer(), col_integer(), col_integer(), col_integer(),
  col_integer())            
)
```

If we do not specify the data type for all the columns, `readr` returns an 
error, which leads to the following questions:

1. What if I want to skip a few columns?
2. What if I want to read certain columns only?

## Select Columns

```{r img9, fig.align='center', echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('img/column_objective_function_map.png')
```

For the first scenario, we use `col_skip()`: instead of specifying the 
data type, we tell `readr` to skip that column while reading the 
data.

For the second scenario, we will use `cols_only()` to specify the 
columns to be read i.e. instead of using `list()` to supply the data types, we 
use `cols_only()` and provide the following details:

- column name
- column type using `col_types` argument

```{r specific_cols}
read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/hsb2.csv', col_types = cols_only(id = col_integer(),
  prog = col_factor(levels = c("1", "2", "3")), read = col_integer())
)
```

If you have a data set with 10 columns and plan to skip only a couple of 
columns, use `col_skip()`. If you plan to read only a couple of columns, use
`cols_only()`.

## Beyond CSV: parquet and quiet reads

Two habits scale beyond this chapter. First, `read_csv()` announces its
guessed column types on every read; once you trust the spec, silence it with
`show_col_types = FALSE`. Second, remote files re-download on every knit;
cache them locally with `download.file()` once and read from disk afterwards.
And when a CSV grows past comfortable memory (the 35 MB `analytics_raw.csv`
in later chapters is the first warning sign), switch the format, not the
workflow: `arrow::read_parquet()` returns the same tibble the dplyr verbs
expect. See @arrow-duckdb for the full quickstart.
